concepts.name: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992: Constitutional Status and Scope
key_dimensions: Distinction between justiciable (compulsory) vs. non-justiciable (voluntary) provisions under Parts IX
Why it added Part IX and Schedule 11 — not Part IV (DPSP) alone
States exempted from applicability: scheduled areas, nagaland, meghalaya, mizoram, hill areas
Difference between 73rd and 74th Amendment Acts in structure and applicability

concepts.name: Three-Tier Structure: Mandatory vs. Discretionary Application
key_dimensions: Article 243B: mandatory constitution of Panchayats at village, intermediate, and district levels
Exception: states with population below 20 lakh may not constitute intermediate tier (Panchayat Samiti)
UPSC trap — which tier is optional and the exact population threshold
Practical examples of states that have opted out of the intermediate tier

concepts.name: Article 243: Definitions — Village, Gram Sabha, Panchayat Area
key_dimensions: Definition of 'village' under Article 243(g) — Governor's power to notify
Gram Sabha vs. Gram Panchayat: constitutional distinction and hierarchy
Article 243(d): definition of 'Panchayat' — elected body vs. administrative body confusion
Why 'intermediate level' definition is flexible and state-determined

concepts.name: Gram Sabha: Constitutional Basis and Sovereign Character
key_dimensions: Article 243A: Gram Sabha as a body of voters at village level — not elected members
Gram Sabha as the foundation of democratic decentralization — often called 'legislature of the village'
Powers of Gram Sabha are state-determined (non-justiciable provision)
PESA Act 1996: enhanced role of Gram Sabha in scheduled areas — approval of development plans, control over minor forest produce

concepts.name: Composition and Direct Elections to Panchayats (Article 243C)
key_dimensions: All seats at all three tiers filled by direct election — key constitutional requirement
Representation of Chairpersons of lower tiers and MPs/MLAs in higher tiers: state legislature's discretion
Distinction: members elected directly vs. chairpersons whose representation is optional
UPSC trap — whether Rajya Sabha/Lok Sabha MPs can be members of district panchayats

concepts.name: Reservation of Seats: Article 243D — SC, ST, and Women
key_dimensions: Mandatory reservation for SCs and STs proportional to their population at each tier and each category of offices
Mandatory not less than one-third reservation for women (including seats reserved for SC/ST women)
State legislature's discretion to provide reservation for OBCs — not constitutionally mandated (key trap)
Rotation of reserved seats: constitutional silence vs. state practice leading to frequent litigation

concepts.name: Reservation of Chairperson Offices: Article 243D(4) and (6)
key_dimensions: Offices of Chairpersons at village, intermediate, and district levels reserved for SC, ST, and women
One-third of total offices of chairpersons reserved for women — mandatory
OBC reservation for chairperson offices: state discretion, not constitutional mandate
Triple test for OBC reservation in local bodies (Supreme Court: Vikas Kishanrao Gawali case, 2021)

concepts.name: Duration of Panchayats and Mid-Term Dissolution: Article 243E
key_dimensions: Five-year term from date of first meeting — not from date of election
Dissolution before expiry of term: elections must be held before expiry OR within 6 months of dissolution
Reconstituted panchayat after dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term
UPSC trap: if remainder term is less than 6 months, elections need not be held

concepts.name: State Election Commission: Article 243K — Appointment, Powers, and Independence
key_dimensions: State Election Commissioner appointed by Governor, removable only like a High Court judge
Superintendence, direction, and control of preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections vested in SEC
SEC is distinct from Election Commission of India — no hierarchical relationship
UPSC trap: delimitation of constituencies is NOT done by SEC but by State Legislature or authority empowered by it

concepts.name: State Finance Commission: Article 243I — Composition and Mandate
key_dimensions: Constituted by Governor every 5 years — mandatory (justiciable provision)
Reviews financial position of Panchayats and recommends distribution of taxes/duties between state and panchayats
Recommendations are not binding on the state government — advisory in nature
Distinction from Central Finance Commission: Article 280(3)(bb) requires CFC to consider SFC recommendations

concepts.name: Eleventh Schedule: 29 Subjects and the 'Devolution' Problem
key_dimensions: Schedule 11 lists 29 functional areas — but devolution is at state legislature's discretion (non-justiciable)
Panchayats have no inherent legislative power — they exercise only delegated functions
UPSC trap: Schedule 11 does not automatically transfer functions; it only guides what states 'may' devolve
Comparison with Schedule 12 (74th Amendment) — 18 subjects for urban local bodies

concepts.name: PESA Act, 1996: Extension of Panchayati Raj to Scheduled (Fifth Schedule) Areas
key_dimensions: PESA extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with modifications protecting tribal self-governance
Gram Sabha given primacy: mandatory consultation for land acquisition, resettlement, minor forest produce
State legislation must be in conformity with PESA — state laws inconsistent with PESA become void
UPSC trap: PESA applies to Fifth Schedule areas only, NOT Sixth Schedule areas (which have autonomous councils)

concepts.name: Disqualifications for Membership: Article 243F and State Discretion
key_dimensions: Disqualifications determined by state legislature — not directly specified in the Constitution
No person disqualified for being less than 25 years if they are 21 years or more (UPSC trap on age)
Minimum age for contesting: 21 years — lower than Parliament (25 for Lok Sabha)
Two-child norm disqualification: upheld by Supreme Court as valid state legislation (Javed v. State of Haryana)

concepts.name: Powers, Authority, and Responsibilities of Panchayats: Article 243G
key_dimensions: State legislature 'may' endow panchayats with powers — entirely discretionary (non-justiciable)
Three Fs of decentralization: Functions, Funds, Functionaries — constitutionally mentioned but not guaranteed
Difference between 'may' provisions and 'shall' provisions in Part IX (justiciable vs. non-justiciable)
Implications of weak devolution: parallel bodies (DRDA, etc.) bypassing panchayats

concepts.name: Audit and Accounts of Panchayats: Article 243J
key_dimensions: State legislature to make provisions for maintenance of accounts and auditing — discretionary
CAG's role in auditing panchayat accounts: depends on state law and nature of funds
Comptroller and Auditor General can audit if grants from consolidated fund of state are involved
Contrast with Article 243Z (municipalities) — same framework for urban local bodies

concepts.name: Bar on Interference by Courts: Article 243O
key_dimensions: No election to panchayat can be questioned except by election petition — bars writ jurisdiction for election disputes
Courts cannot interfere in electoral process once it has commenced (similar to Article 329 for Parliament)
Delimitation orders under Part IX not questionable in any court
UPSC trap: Article 243O does not bar judicial review of legislative actions, only election disputes

concepts.name: Exempted States and Areas: Applicability Exceptions under Article 243M
key_dimensions: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram: fully exempt due to customary law and traditional structures
Hill areas of Manipur and districts of Darjeeling (West Bengal): partially exempt
Scheduled areas (Fifth Schedule) and tribal areas (Sixth Schedule): different treatment
UPSC trap: Sixth Schedule areas are fully exempt while Fifth Schedule areas are covered through PESA

concepts.name: Continuity of Existing Laws and Panchayats: Article 243N (Transitional Provisions)
key_dimensions: Existing panchayat laws to continue for one year after 73rd Amendment's commencement or until amended
Panchayats already constituted to continue until expiry of their term
Transitional nature: Article 243N resolved potential conflict between old state acts and new constitutional mandate
Relevance to states that had Panchayati Raj before 1993 (e.g., Rajasthan, Maharashtra)

concepts.name: Relationship Between Panchayats and State Legislature: Supervisory Framework
key_dimensions: Panchayati Raj is a state subject (Entry 5, List II) — Centre has no direct legislative power
State can dissolve, supersede, or reconstitute panchayats — subject to Article 243E safeguards
State government can issue directions and the panchayat has no immunity from state executive control
Contrast with constitutional bodies like CAG or EC which have independent constitutional protection

concepts.name: Devolution Index and Comparative Performance of States
key_dimensions: Ministry of Panchayati Raj's Devolution Index ranks states on transfer of 3Fs
Kerala and Karnataka cited as models; Bihar and UP as laggards — basis of Mains analytical questions
Parallel bodies (e.g., District Rural Development Agency) as institutional competitors undermining panchayats
15th Finance Commission recommendations: tied vs. untied grants to panchayats and conditionalities
